title: NormedAddTorsor: The Abstract Setting for Euclidean Geometry
mathContext: The proof works in a `NormedAddTorsor V P` — a Euclidean space abstraction where $P$ is a 'torsor' over a vector space $V$. The key operations are `vsub : P → P → V` (subtraction: $A -_v B \in V$) and `vadd : V → P → P` (translation: $v +_v A \in P$). This cleanly separates points ($P$, no origin) from vectors ($V$, has origin).
significance: The `NormedAddTorsor` abstraction is essential: it allows the proof to work for any Euclidean space of any dimension, not just $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $\mathbb{R}^n$ for specific $n$. The variables `[NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P]` set up a fully general inner product geometry framework in which all Euclidean theorems can be proved once.

title: vsub_eq_apex_diff: The Apex Vector Decomposition
mathContext: The lemma proves $C -_v B = (A -_v B) - (A -_v C)$ — the base vector equals the difference of the two apex-to-base vectors. The proof uses two torsor identities: `vsub_add_vsub_cancel C A B : (C -_v A) + (A -_v B) = C -_v B` and `neg_vsub_eq_vsub_rev A C : -(A -_v C) = C -_v A`, combined via `abel` to handle the abelian group arithmetic.
significance: This is the key structural lemma underlying Pappus's proof. Geometrically: if $p = A -_v B$ and $q = A -_v C$ are the 'apex vectors' (from base vertices back to apex), then the base vector $C -_v B = p - q$. This means the angle $\angle ABC$ (between $A -_v B$ and $C -_v B$) equals $\mathrm{angle}(p, p-q)$, and $\angle ACB = \mathrm{angle}(q, q-p)$, setting up the symmetry argument.
relatedConcepts: abel tactic for abelian group goals
prerequisites: abel tactic for linear arithmetic in abelian groups

title: pappus_isosceles: Four Lines Capturing 2000 Years of Insight
mathContext:
The proof of $\angle ABC = \angle ACB$ from `dist A B = dist A C` is:
1. `show` unfolds `EuclideanGeometry.angle` to `InnerProductGeometry.angle (A -_v B) (C -_v B) = ...`
2. `rw [vsub_eq_apex_diff, vsub_neg_eq_apex_diff]` rewrites base vectors as $p-q$ and $q-p$
3. `apply InnerProductGeometry.angle_sub_eq_angle_sub_rev_of_norm_eq` gives $\mathrm{angle}(p,p-q) = \mathrm{angle}(q,q-p)$ for $\|p\| = \|q\|$
4. `simpa only [← dist_eq_norm_vsub] using h` converts the dist hypothesis to the norm hypothesis.
significance: The Mathlib lemma `angle_sub_eq_angle_sub_rev_of_norm_eq` is the algebraic crystallization of Pappus's observation: equal-norm vectors have a symmetric angle relationship with their difference. The `show` tactic is needed to make `EuclideanGeometry.angle` (the geometric notion) definitionally equal to `InnerProductGeometry.angle` (the algebraic notion) visible to Lean's unifier.

title: euclid_outer_segs_eq: Step 1 of Euclid's Four-Step Proof
mathContext: In Euclid's original proof, auxiliary points $F$ and $G$ are placed beyond $B$ and $C$ on extensions of $AB$ and $AC$, with $AF = AG$. The first claim is $BF = CG$ (the outer segments are equal). Here, $AF = s \cdot AB$ and $AG = t \cdot AC$, so $AF = AG$ and $AB = AC$ together force $s = t$, giving $BF = (s-1) \cdot AB = (t-1) \cdot AC = CG$. The `calc` proof assembles this as: $(s-1) \cdot AB = sAB - AB = tAB - AB = (t-1)AB = (t-1)AC$.
significance: This lemma documents only the first step of Euclid's four-step proof. The full Euclid proof would continue: prove $\triangle AFC \cong \triangle AGB$ (SAS), then $\triangle BFC \cong \triangle CGB$ (using $BF=CG$ from this step), then subtract angles. Lean's `calc` block handles the algebra cleanly with `ring` and a single `rw [hAB_eq_AC]` hypothesis substitution.
prerequisites: Euclid's auxiliary construction for Pons Asinorum

title: euclid_i5: The Alias Connecting Both Names to One Proof
mathContext: `theorem euclid_i5 ... := pappus_isosceles h` is a one-line alias that makes the theorem discoverable under both Euclid's name (I.5) and Pappus's name. The theorem statement is identical: `dist A B = dist A C → ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B`.
significance: The `#check @pappus_isosceles` and `#check @euclid_i5` commands at lines 141-142 serve as documentation — they verify both names are in scope with the correct types. Naming the same result twice reflects the historical duality: the theorem is Euclid's but Pappus's proof is simpler. This design choice makes both names searchable in future Mathlib contributions.
